title: The Ethics of Moral Luck
paragraphs: Two equally reckless drivers, one who arrives home safely and another whose identical recklessness happens to result in a fatal accident, receive dramatically different moral and legal judgment despite behaving identically, a puzzle philosophers term moral luck.

This asymmetry challenges intuitive assumptions that moral responsibility should track only factors genuinely within an individual's control, since the outcome distinguishing these two drivers depended entirely on circumstances neither driver actually controlled or could have reasonably anticipated.

Some philosophers argue this asymmetry reveals an inconsistency in ordinary moral judgment that careful ethical reasoning should correct, suggesting that identical underlying conduct deserves identical moral assessment regardless of resulting outcome, however severe.

Others defend the asymmetry as reflecting a legitimate, if imperfectly theorized, moral intuition that actual consequences matter independently of intention or care taken, arguing that a purely intention-based ethics fails to capture something genuinely important about moral experience.

This unresolved tension reflects a deeper disagreement about whether moral responsibility should track only controllable factors or should also incorporate consequences that, however uncontrolled, remain undeniably real and significant to those actually affected.

Practical legal and social systems generally compromise between these positions, assigning greater consequence to worse outcomes while still incorporating intention and recklessness as independently relevant factors, an uneasy but perhaps unavoidable synthesis of two genuinely competing moral intuitions.
